structure.title: III.A First National Survey (design and results)
III.B Discussion: Why Are Social Norms Misperceived?

observations.statement: The main experiment is described as a two-stage field experiment: an in-person session with individual-level random assignment to an information treatment about others' opinions, followed by a separate phone follow-up survey to capture longer-term outcomes.

Randomization of the information treatment is implemented at the individual level using the last three digits of each participant's phone number, pre-assigned to treatment values before sessions began, a procedure the paper says avoids recording identifying information alongside responses.

The recruitment experiment is framed as a natural field experiment embedded directly in a private firm's real hiring process, holding the employer, task, and pay structure fixed while randomizing only the home/outside-home framing and whether applicants hear the social-norm information.

The main experiment sample is recruited through a local branch of an international survey company using a recruiter database, snowball sampling, and street intercept across Riyadh neighborhoods, with the unit of observation being the married male respondent and, through him, his wife's later labor-supply outcomes.

A pilot round of sessions run just before the main experiment is explicitly excluded from the analysis sample, and participants who did not complete the second half of the online survey are dropped, with both exclusions justified in footnotes rather than in the main text.

Follow-up respondents are linked back to their original session responses using only session number plus trailing phone digits; pairs sharing identical trailing digits within a session are dropped because they cannot be uniquely matched, and overall follow-up attrition is reported and checked for selectivity.
observations.quote: no evidence of selective attrition overall

observations.statement: Two additional national online surveys and a public opinion survey supply separate samples used for external validity and mechanism checks, each with its own sample composition reported alongside the corresponding table or figure rather than pooled into the main experiment's tables.

The main behavioral outcome, signing the wife up for a job-matching service, is coded so that anyone who initially opts in but then withholds the wife's contact details is recoded as not having signed up, a construction the paper states was decided in advance.

A 'wedge' variable is constructed as each respondent's guessed share of session peers agreeing with the statement minus the true share agreeing, and is used both to describe the extent of misperception and, split by its sign, to define heterogeneity subgroups.

Follow-up outcomes are combined into a single standardized index following an established neighborhood-effects methodology, expressed in control-group standard-deviation units, explicitly to address the multiplicity of outcomes collected in the follow-up call.

The main sign-up regression table adds session fixed effects, then baseline-belief controls, then socioeconomic controls across successive columns, with sample size and R-squared reported in rows at the foot of each column and fixed-effect and control sets marked by checkmarks.

Table notes state that the headline standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust, while an accompanying inference-robustness block beneath each coefficient separately reports p-values from a session-clustered wild bootstrap and from a permutation test, with the bootstrap clustering level specified only in the notes.

The same baseline-then-variants column structure used in the main sign-up table is repeated for the follow-up outcomes table, the wedge-heterogeneity table, the belief-update table, and the recruitment-experiment table, giving a uniform reporting template across all main regression tables.

Rather than a separate mean-of-dependent-variable row, the control-group level of each outcome is conveyed through the regression constant and, more prominently, through the labeled bars of companion bar-chart figures placed alongside each table.

The paper justifies reporting session-clustered wild cluster bootstrap p-values by pointing to the small number of experimental sessions, citing a methodological reference on inference with clustered errors and few clusters.
observations.quote: wild cluster bootstrap standard errors because of the small number of clusters

observations.statement: Permutation-based p-values are reported alongside robust and bootstrap standard errors in every main table, motivated in a footnote by concern about small subsample sizes rather than by any clustering structure.

Because many follow-up outcomes are collected, the paper reports p-values adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing using an experimental-economics procedure, presented as an extra row in the follow-up outcomes table rather than replacing the unadjusted p-values.

Although the information treatment is randomized at the individual level within sessions, the robustness bootstrap standard errors are clustered at the session level, treating shared physical location and social network as the relevant clustering unit rather than the randomization unit itself.

A balance table comparing respondent characteristics across the control and treatment arms of the main experiment is placed in the main text immediately before the headline results, its purpose stated as confirming that randomization succeeded.
observations.quote: confirming that the randomization was successful

observations.statement: Selective attrition between the main experiment and the follow-up call is checked against observable characteristics and against the original sign-up decision, with the supporting tables placed in an online appendix that is outside the scope of this reading.
observations.locator: Sec. I.A; online Appendix Tables B1-B2 (not available)

observations.statement: Lower and upper attrition bounds following an established sample-selection bounding method are computed for every follow-up treatment effect and reported as extra rows directly inside the main results table rather than in a separate bounds table.

A placebo check on a filler question about the minimum wage, unrelated to the gender-norm treatment, is reported in an online appendix figure and described in the main text as showing no treatment effect, supporting the claim that the intervention updated norm-specific beliefs rather than beliefs in general.
observations.locator: footnote 26; online Appendix Figure B3 (not available)

observations.statement: Balance checks for the first national survey and for the recruitment experiment are each reported in a dedicated online appendix table, following the same balance-table convention used for the main experiment but kept out of the main text.
observations.locator: online Appendix Tables B9, B11 (not available)

observations.statement: Rather than a dedicated robustness section, every main coefficient in every regression table is accompanied by a fixed three-way robustness block reporting p-values from robust, session-bootstrapped, and permutation-based standard errors directly beneath the point estimate.

Heterogeneity by the sign of the belief wedge is treated as a robustness and mechanism check at once: the sample is split into those who initially underestimated versus overestimated peer support, with separate columns and a companion figure for each subgroup.

A robustness check restricting the sample to respondents who originally held private views supportive of the outcome of interest is reported only in a footnote, described as leaving the point estimate essentially unchanged.

A continuous belief-update measure, equal to the negative of the wedge for treated respondents and zero for controls, is used in a separate specification to show that larger updates in perceived norms are associated with larger increases in the take-up outcome.

Heterogeneity by number of social connections within the session and by presence of children in the household is examined and reported as showing no striking pattern, with the detailed figures placed in an online appendix rather than the main tables.
observations.locator: footnote 29, footnote 31; online Appendix Figures B5-B7 (not available)

observations.statement: An alternative labor-demand-signaling channel is tested by checking whether the information treatment shifts beliefs about firms' willingness to hire women and whether that belief correlates with the take-up decision; the paper concludes this channel is not driving the results, based on appendix tables.
observations.locator: Sec. IIC; online Appendix Tables B7-B8 (not available)

observations.statement: A lack-of-communication mechanism is probed using a separate survey question on how often respondents discuss the topic with male friends and relatives, showing a near-monotonic relationship between discussion frequency and the size of the perception wedge, explicitly labeled as suggestive and open to a reverse-causality interpretation.

A correlation between how many other session participants a respondent knows and how accurate that respondent's guess is presented as consistent with social learning about the norm, while the text explicitly flags that the same pattern could instead reflect homophily rather than communication.
observations.locator: Sec. IIA; online Appendix Figure B2 (not available)

observations.statement: Treatment effects throughout the results sections are interpreted primarily as a percentage-point change and as a proportional change relative to the corresponding control-group baseline level, rather than in standardized effect-size units.

The continuous belief-update specification is interpreted by translating a one-standard-deviation move in the update measure into an implied change in the take-up probability, giving a magnitude benchmark distinct from the simple treatment-control comparisons used elsewhere.

The paper explicitly flags that the study is not powered to detect a significant change in the wife's actual employment outside the home, distinguishing this from the two job-search outcomes for which significant effects are reported.
observations.quote: not powered to detect a significant change in the likelihood

observations.statement: The authors acknowledge they cannot cleanly separate a persistent reduction in perceived stigma from a mechanical effect of easier job-service access in explaining the longer-term outcomes, and that within-session communication between treated and control participants could have diluted the measured treatment-control gap in beliefs.

The conclusion notes the study only elicits and acts on husbands' perceptions and decisions, not wives' own opinions, and flags this as an open direction rather than a limitation the current design can address.

External validity of the core misperception finding is supported by triangulating across the original experimental sample, two independently recruited national surveys, and an existing nationally representative public-opinion survey conducted years earlier, rather than by a single representativeness claim.

The recruitment experiment is explicitly characterized as a proof of concept for policy-relevant scaling of the information intervention rather than as evidence about effects at the scale of a labor market, and the conclusion repeats this framing when discussing future work.

Headline treatment effects are shown as paired bar charts of control versus treatment percentages with binomial confidence intervals and an equality-of-proportions p-value printed above the bars, used as the primary presentation device before the corresponding regression table is shown.

None of the regression tables use significance stars; instead every coefficient is followed by a labeled inference-robustness block giving three separate p-values, and the table notes spell out exactly which standard-error method and clustering choice each p-value corresponds to.

The summary-statistics table reports means with standard deviations in parentheses for the full sample and separately by arm, and its note specifies exactly which follow-up subsample underlies the one variable that is not observed in the main experiment itself.

Distributional evidence on misperception is conveyed through a kernel-density plot of the belief wedge in the main experiment and, in the national survey, through cumulative-distribution plots of guesses overlaid with vertical lines marking the true proportions, rather than through histograms or single summary statistics alone.

The introduction previews the direction and substance of every major result, from the extent of misperception through the follow-up labor-supply outcomes and the recruitment-experiment findings, before any design or methodology is described.

A contribution paragraph situating the paper against literatures on cultural persistence, gender and labor markets, and social-image concerns is followed immediately by an explicit paragraph mapping each numbered section of the paper to its content, both placed at the close of the introduction.

Discussion of competing mechanisms for the main-experiment results is placed in its own subsection immediately after the main results and heterogeneity subsections, before the paper moves on to the separate national-survey material.

Robustness figures, balance tables, placebo checks, and several heterogeneity breakdowns are consistently pushed into a numbered online appendix referenced from the main text rather than reproduced inline, so the main text stays focused on the primary chain of results.
observations.locator: throughout, references to online Appendix A-C

observations.statement: A replication data record deposited with the American Economic Association is cited in the reference list under the corresponding author byline, following the standard AEA data-and-code repository citation format rather than an in-text data-availability statement.
The only software named in the main text is the commercial survey platform used to field the experiment and surveys; no statistical or analysis software is named in the body of the paper itself.
observations.quote: administered using the online survey software Qualtrics

observations.statement: All analysis data are either newly collected by the authors through their own experiments and surveys or drawn from a pre-existing publicly documented cross-national opinion survey used only for external benchmarking, with no restricted administrative microdata used anywhere in the paper.
observations.locator: Sec. IIIA, Evidence from the Arab Barometer

observations.statement: A footnote directs readers to the article's online DOI landing page for additional materials and author disclosure statements, pointing to a general journal mechanism for supplementary access rather than describing a specific data-request procedure in the text itself.

Institutional ethics approval is stated in a single sentence in the acknowledgments footnote naming the approving university review board, with no separate discussion of ethical considerations or risks elsewhere in the paper.
observations.quote: approved by the University of Chicago Institutional Review

observations.statement: The main experiment, its follow-up survey, and the later recruitment experiment are each identified by a separate registry number in a public trials registry, cited together in the opening acknowledgments footnote rather than discussed individually where each design is introduced.

The two outcomes analyzed in the recruitment experiment are explicitly labeled as pre-registered at the point they are introduced, distinguishing them from the more exploratory heterogeneity and mechanism analyses conducted elsewhere in the paper.

concordance.paper_says: All main specifications are estimated by OLS, per Table 2 notes ('Column 1 reports estimates from an OLS regression...').
Column 2 of Table 2 adds session fixed effects, per the table notes.
Robust standard errors are the reported baseline SE type, per Table 2 notes.
Wild bootstrap p-values are clustered at the session level, per Table 2 notes and footnote 25.
concordance.card_shows: s1.se.cluster_level=null; the card's se object records only the baseline robust SE and does not capture the session-clustered wild-bootstrap variant.
concordance.note: The card's field for the primary specification's SE object has a null cluster level even though the paper states a session-level cluster for the supplementary bootstrap p-values.

concordance.paper_says: Column 4 adds socioeconomic controls: age, education, employment status of respondent and wife, number of children, and share of session participants known or with mutual friends, per Table 2 notes.
concordance.card_shows: s4.controls_summary='baseline beliefs, employment, education, household characteristics'.

concordance.paper_says: Table 4 splits the sample by the sign of the wedge (underestimators versus overestimators) as the heterogeneity comparison.
concordance.card_shows: s5.notes describes a Table 4 heterogeneity variant by sign of the belief-reality gap (wedge).

concordance.paper_says: Table 2 column 4 has a smaller observation count than columns 1-3 because of missing covariates, shown in the observations row.
concordance.card_shows: s4.sample=null; the card does not record a sample description for this specification.

concordance.paper_says: Table 1 in the main text reports a balance table across arms, described as confirming successful randomization.
concordance.card_shows: x1.status=not_found_in_scope; the code producing the balance table was not located within the files the extraction read.
concordance.note: The card's partial code coverage did not include the script producing Table 1; the gap reflects coverage limits rather than a code/paper conflict.

concordance.paper_says: The follow-up sample is restricted to matched respondents and Lee (2009) attrition bounds are reported for every follow-up outcome.
concordance.card_shows: x2 confirms a 'keep if matched == 1' restriction and a leebounds command call in the follow-up script.

concordance.paper_says: A Kling-Liebman-Katz index and List-Shaikh-Xu multiple-hypothesis-testing-adjusted p-values are reported for the follow-up outcomes.
concordance.card_shows: x3 confirms an mhtexp command call applied to the constructed index.

concordance.paper_says: Session-clustered wild cluster bootstrap standard errors are reported as an inference-robustness check in every main table.
concordance.card_shows: robustness entry: alt_se via a boottest command, baseline spec s1, relationship_status=unresolved.
concordance.note: The card marks the code-side relationship to s1 as unresolved even though the practice itself (a session-clustered wild bootstrap) is confirmed present in both paper and code.

concordance.paper_says: Permutation tests are reported for all coefficients, and the wedge-sign heterogeneity split in Table 4 uses the same permutation-inference approach.
concordance.card_shows: robustness entry: alt_se via a permute command, baseline specs s1-s4, variant spec s5, relationship_status=confirmed.

concordance.paper_says: Table 2 in the printed paper is the main sign-up regression table.
concordance.card_shows: t1.path=output/table2.tex, produced via an esttab call.

gaps: No formal numbered estimating equation is given anywhere in the text; all specifications are described in prose and in table notes only.
No explicit ex ante power calculation is reported; the power limitation for the wife's-employment outcome is stated only as an ex post observation.
No informed-consent procedure is described for the main experiment's in-person participants (only IRB approval is stated); an online consent form is mentioned only for the later national survey.
No pre-analysis-plan deviations are discussed; pre-registration is cited by registry number but the text never states whether any planned analysis was changed.
No statistical analysis software (e.g., Stata) is named anywhere in the main text; only the survey-fielding platform (Qualtrics) is identified.

reading.note: Read the full extracted text end to end, including all footnotes, table and figure notes, and the reference list (33 pages of main text plus references; this is the complete supplied text/PDF). The paper's online Appendix A-C and appendix tables/figures B1-B11, referenced throughout, are not part of the supplied PDF/text and were not read; observations that rely on appendix content are tagged online_appendix_not_available and record only what the main text states the appendix contains.
